items.streamTitle: A nationwide RCT cut electricity modestly—but only some households responded
items.streamSummary: A six-month randomized trial of 62,750 Saudi households found that peer-comparison messages combined with energy-saving tips reduced monthly electricity use by roughly 1–2%. The effect was concentrated among moderate-consumption households, with little measurable change at the lowest and highest consumption levels. Because the outcome came from smart meters, this is real behavioral evidence rather than intention. It also shows why a small average effect can conceal major differences in who has the opportunity or capacity to respond.
items.attribution: Darandary — International Review of Economics & Finance

items.streamTitle: A low polarization score can hide very different audience states
items.streamSummary: Across three nationally representative U.S. surveys, researchers found that people with similarly low affective-polarization scores could be politically very different: some were relatively lukewarm toward both parties, while others were cold toward both. Those groups differed in trust, participation, democratic attitudes, and demographics. The study is descriptive rather than causal, but it shows how a convenient difference score can erase meaningful structure that matters for audience segmentation.

items.streamTitle: Do not invent your agents’ belief structure when empirical data can seed it
items.streamSummary: SimPol builds belief networks from survey data across 23 European countries and uses those empirically inferred structures to initialize an agent-based polarization model. The simulated dynamics then vary with parameters such as belief rigidity and susceptibility to social influence. The architecture is valuable because it separates empirical baseline structure from theory-driven update rules instead of inventing synthetic agents from scratch. It remains a preprint, and matching broad patterns is not the same as demonstrating causal or predictive validity.

items.streamTitle: An FCM edge does not have to be one number
items.streamSummary: KA-FCM replaces each static Fuzzy Cognitive Map edge weight with an inspectable learned function, allowing the relationship between two variables to include thresholds, saturation, or even sign reversals. In computational tests it handled nonmonotonic relationships better than conventional FCMs while keeping the edge behavior visible. The approach is still a preprint, and fitting a flexible function from data does not solve confounding or causal identification, but it offers a useful route beyond constant-sign scalar edges.

items.streamTitle: Moral licensing largely disappeared when nobody was watching
items.streamSummary: A preregistered meta-analysis of 115 experiments found that moral licensing—doing something good and then behaving less morally—was much stronger when people knew they were being observed. After adjustment for publication bias, the authors found moderate evidence for licensing under explicit observation but evidence against a meaningful effect when behavior was unobserved. The result suggests that reputation and audience presence may be central boundary conditions rather than background noise.
items.attribution: Rotella et al. — Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin

items.streamTitle: Moral language can help engagement—until it becomes too dense
items.streamSummary: An analysis of more than 1.6 million posts across Twitter, Reddit, and 8chan found a nonlinear relationship between moral language and engagement. Overall moral relevance was associated with more engagement, but concentrating too much moral content into a message was associated with less; engagement peaked at an intermediate density. The result challenges “more is better” assumptions in message optimization, although the study is observational and does not prove that experimentally increasing moral density would cause the same change.
items.attribution: Candia et al. — Nature Human Behaviour

items.streamTitle: Germany’s drone attribution moved from accusation to a cost-imposition package
items.streamSummary: Germany’s attribution of the Leipzig/Halle drone incident was followed by concrete diplomatic measures and discussion of additional EU sanctions, while Russia denied responsibility. The development is useful because it shows attribution becoming an intervention package rather than remaining a statement about responsibility. The downstream effects are still open questions: imposed costs and allied endorsement do not themselves demonstrate deterrence or a change in future adversary behavior.

items.streamTitle: LLMs can estimate average social norms well—but their errors look like a shared hivemind
items.streamSummary: A benchmark of 555 everyday U.S. scenarios found that several LLMs estimated population-average social norms more accurately than individual humans. But human errors were mostly independent, so pooling people improved estimates dramatically, while errors across LLMs were much more correlated and model ensembles added little. A hybrid human-plus-LLM estimate performed best. The result supports a bounded use for models as aggregate prior estimators and warns against treating multiple LLM personas as independent evidence about population diversity.
items.attribution: Eriksson et al. — Communications AI & Computing

items.streamTitle: People do not automatically model their audience—but scaffolding can help
items.streamSummary: Three experiments found that people use a mix of sophisticated audience modeling and simpler heuristics when deciding what information to teach. Many participants persisted with a heuristic even after it stopped working, but a task that made it easier to infer what the learner knew substantially reduced that tendency. The finding suggests that poor audience analysis can result from cognitive demands, not just missing data, and that communication tools can improve performance by scaffolding the inference itself.
items.attribution: Harootonian et al. — Nature Human Behaviour

items.streamTitle: Coalition causal discovery needs semantic and intervention governance
items.streamSummary: FLODO reframes causal discovery for settings where different agents see different variables, use different labels, and cannot simply pool all raw data. The protocol lets local agents exchange structural information while humans manage intervention strategy, semantic alignment, and disputed edges. It also treats simultaneous interventions as a source of contamination. The contribution is highly relevant to coalition and interagency analysis, although the peer-reviewed protocol remains an early framework rather than a broadly validated operational system.

items.streamTitle: A dynamic FCM reconstructed famine-like conditions that static thresholds missed
items.streamSummary: A retrospective Fuzzy Cognitive Map integrated 21 factors and 74 weighted relationships to reconstruct the 2017 Ayod County famine crisis. The model generated a famine-like trajectory during months that later survey evidence supported, even though the area was never formally classified as famine by the static IPC process. The case illustrates how a dynamic systems model can integrate sparse evidence and feedback over time, while its largely expert-defined weights remain hypotheses rather than identified causal effects.
items.attribution: Matthew Day — Journal of Public Health Policy

items.streamTitle: ROK–U.S. I2E2 treats information effects as a coordination-system problem
items.streamSummary: The inaugural ROK–U.S. I2E2 tabletop exercise organized work around countering foreign disinformation, synchronizing cyber/space/electromagnetic responses, and aligning strategic communication across agencies and coalition partners. The important shift is upstream: the exercise treats coordination architecture, timing, attribution, and cross-domain consistency as part of the information-effect system. The official report documents process and institutionalization, not evidence that the resulting communications changed audience behavior.

items.streamTitle: LLMs may be useful experiment forecasters even when they are not valid synthetic participants
items.streamSummary: A Nature validation study compared GPT-4 forecasts with hundreds of treatment effects from real preregistered experiments. The model captured the relative pattern of effects surprisingly well and performed similarly to pooled human forecasts, including on some studies unavailable before its training cutoff. It also systematically overestimated effect sizes. That makes the most defensible use case a screening layer—helping prioritize what to test—rather than treating simulated responses as empirical human evidence.

items.streamTitle: A truthful norm correction can move public and private behavior in different directions
items.streamSummary: A randomized experiment corrected participants’ beliefs about how many Americans support carbon taxation. The correction improved norm accuracy but did not increase average private climate donations; among people who had overestimated support, donations actually fell. At the same time, treated participants became more willing to take a publicly observable action. The study shows why norm interventions need baseline beliefs and behavior type: the same accurate information can have different—and sometimes opposite—effects across audiences and outcomes.
items.attribution: Galdikiene, Jaraite & Kajackaite — Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization

items.streamTitle: Physical proximity on the Senate floor measurably shifted real votes
items.streamSummary: An NBER natural experiment exploits U.S. Senate seating assignments to estimate peer influence on actual legislative votes. Senators seated near one another shifted each other’s voting by an estimated 11.9 percentage points, with effects concentrated within about 20 feet; computer-vision analysis of C-SPAN footage showed more face-to-face interaction among nearby members. The study highlights physical exposure opportunity as a real influence variable, while the observed interaction process is supporting mechanism evidence rather than a separately randomized mediator.

items.streamTitle: Turning an algorithmic feed on changed attitudes and follow networks; turning it off did not simply reverse them
items.streamSummary: A seven-week randomized field experiment among active U.S. X users found that switching people from a chronological to an algorithmic feed increased engagement, shifted some political attitudes in a conservative direction, and led participants to follow more conservative activist accounts. Moving existing algorithmic-feed users to chronological feeds did not create an equal and opposite effect. The asymmetry matters because an exposure regime can alter the follow network that determines later exposure, creating path dependence beyond the immediate feed treatment.

items.streamTitle: Public attribution turns an intelligence judgment into a strategic intervention
items.streamSummary: German officials moved toward publicly blaming Russia for an attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, according to Reuters, while signaling possible consequences. The important analytical point is not only who is blamed: public attribution itself can shape allied cohesion, public threat perception, support for countermeasures, and adversary expectations. Because the underlying intelligence is not fully public and Moscow denied responsibility, the attribution claim should remain distinct from independently established ground truth.

items.streamTitle: Defensive states can change how threat and reward are weighed
items.streamSummary: A high-precision neuroscience study found that threat-related cardiac slowing was associated with stronger weighting of both threat and reward during approach–avoidance decisions. Neural value signals also predicted choices before the overt response. The result complicates the simple idea that stronger defensive reactions always mean more avoidance: physiological state may change how competing information is integrated. The evidence is strong for the laboratory task but should not be generalized directly to real-world crisis or deterrence decisions.

items.streamTitle: Behavioral theory needs a formalization layer before it becomes an agent rule
items.streamSummary: MOZAIC provides a systematic way to translate verbal social-science theories into mathematical decision rules for agent-based models. The authors demonstrate the method with rational choice, bounded rationality, habit, prospect theory, and descriptive norms, producing reusable mathematical building blocks. The contribution addresses a common problem: two simulations can cite the same theory but implement it very differently. Formalization makes those choices inspectable, though it does not prove that a particular mathematical function is correct for a target population.

items.streamTitle: Influence simulation needs networks and narrative dynamics—not just personas
items.streamSummary: The LAND/GhostField demonstration simulated more than 314,000 cyber-social agents and human actors exchanging over half a million messages across a month-long synthetic scenario. Its central design choice is important: influence emerges from the interaction of network structure, repeated exposure, and evolving discourse rather than from persona traits alone. The scale and architecture are notable, but the scenario remains synthetic; convincing emergent agent behavior is not evidence that real populations would behave the same way.

items.streamTitle: LLM social simulation needs a protocol and an audit trail
items.streamSummary: MASS turns LLM-agent role-play into a more explicit research protocol by specifying roles, information boundaries, round schedules, scenario rules, structured outputs, logs, model versions, and validation targets. The framework was demonstrated across three real-world-inspired cases and is designed to make simulations easier to audit and reproduce. Its authors appropriately frame it as mechanism rehearsal and research-design preparation rather than a replacement for experiments or causal inference.

items.streamTitle: Community Notes sharply reduced later reposting—but often arrived after the viral phase
items.streamSummary: A large quasi-experimental study of 237,180 fact-checked cascades on X estimated that Community Notes reduced subsequent reposting by 61.2% after display and substantially increased author deletion. The catch was timing: notes often appeared only after a post had already experienced its fastest growth. The study therefore separates treatment efficacy from system effectiveness. A correction can work once delivered and still have limited total impact if it arrives too late.

items.streamTitle: A major influencer measurably shifted high-stakes university-major choices
items.streamSummary: A natural experiment using more than 3.3 million Chinese admissions observations linked a prominent influencer’s public advice to changes in real university-major choices. A negative signal about Journalism and Communication was followed by substantially worse admission ranks, especially at elite universities, while an endorsed field saw smaller positive effects. The design includes event-study and placebo checks, making this unusually strong evidence on consequential behavior, though the specific psychological mechanism and transfer to other contexts remain less certain.

items.streamTitle: Peer praise changed behavior without increasing the empathy it was designed to activate
items.streamSummary: A large Registered Report tested peer praise as a way to motivate empathy toward racial outgroups. Average empathy and willingness to engage empathically did not increase, yet participants became more likely to write letters advocating racial equality. That mismatch is the important result: an intervention can affect behavior even when the mechanism it was designed around does not move. The study is a strong reminder not to infer how an intervention worked from its label or intent.
